extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of comparative mythology / folklore
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and describe the characteristics, origins, and evolution of 'departmental' deities (sun, thunder, sea, moon, agricultural, fire, wind, earth) in comparative mythology, with illustrative examples and folkloric continuities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Departmental type of deity (general formation)
rubrics_metrics.description: How a strictly 'departmental' type of deity arises: begins as a mere elemental or eponymous spirit (corn-, sun-, water-, thunder-spirit etc.), then gains wider reverence, numerous attributes, more involved ritual, and moral/ethical ideas until possessing a sanctified human character and more-than-human powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original passage: 'At first he is a mere corn-spirit, maize-spirit, earth-spirit, water-, thunder-, sun-spirit, or what not... but as generations pass his fame grows and attracts wider reverence. His attributes become numerous, his ritual more involved; and the wondrous sentiment of the sacred surrounds him with a mystic veil. Ethical ideas become attached to his worship; he is regarded as a fount of righteousness...' Use this lifecycle as the analytic criterion when tracing deity origins: look for elemental/functional origin → accumulation of attributes → ritual elaboration → individualization and anthropomorphism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Animistic vs anthropomorphic distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish between animistic conceptions (the luminary or element itself considered alive/personified) and later anthropomorphic 'man of the X' deities (a human-like god dwelling in/associated with the element rather than being the element).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and note: Peruvian solar worshippers saw the sun as a living thing; Apollo functions as a cultural/solar hero distinct from Helios who is 'the sun himself'. The analyst must 'distinguish between the anthropomorphic "man of the sun" and the merely animistic concept of the sun-god.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Sun-god attributes and typical solar myth pattern
rubrics_metrics.description: Characteristics and recurrent mythic narrative of sun-figures: birth from darkness/dawn, casting off mists/swaddling, journey across the sky gaining strength to zenith then declining, combat with a night/underworld monster, descent through the Underworld and eventual re-emergence at dawn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the provided synopsis as an identification template: 'After the sun has risen... he pursues his course... having passed the zenith, he gradually declines... encounters the monster night, who fights with and devours him. He must then traverse the Underworld... until he succeeds in emerging once more at the gates of morning.' Compare variants (Apollo, Helios, Egyptian sun-boat, Merodach, Ama-terasu, Beowulf, Arthurian analogues). Be alert for later allegorical layers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thunder-gods: origins, apparatus, and associations
rubrics_metrics.description: Thunder-gods often originate from animistic animal/bird forms (thunder-bird), retain avian/animal traces in transitional forms, and possess apparatus by which thunder is produced (beating wings, sheets of metal, hammer, chariot wheels). They commonly bear lightning weapons (spear/arrow), are associated with war and the chase, and may also have agricultural/rain-bringing functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Uitzilopochtli (bird-origin), Thor (hammer/chariot), Zeus/Jupiter (bolts forged by Titans), Indra (quail shape, steals heavenly liquor). Note serpent imagery linking lightning to rain ('Cloud-serpent'). Investigate dual roles: fertilizing (rain) and martial (war patron).

rubrics_metrics.name: Marine deities: piscine form and protean roles
rubrics_metrics.description: Sea-gods often retain piscine/eponymous fish origins and are depicted as anthropomorphic figures with fish-tails; they preside over the 'harvest of the waste of waters' and, with the rise of navigation, acquire protective/destructive control over storms, winds, and voyages, extending authority to estuaries, lakes, rivers, and brooks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instances: Copacahuana (Peruvian fish-bodied idol), Poseidon/Neptune, Oannes/Ea. Trace links between subsistence (fish as food supply) and deity form; look for later expansion of powers with maritime activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lunar gods: growth, time, water, fertility, and wisdom associations
rubrics_metrics.description: Moon-deities are commonly linked with vegetable growth (night continuation of sun's work), time-reckoning (lunar calendars), dew/dampness and therefore water/rain, fertility and love (patronage of courtship), and in some traditions wisdom or record-keeping (e.g., Thoth).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Mexican conflation of moon and water words, Egyptian Thoth as god of writing/wisdom, Artemis/Diana as huntress and harvest/fertility patron. Also note negative attributions (mother of ghosts, miasmatic fogs) in some traditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agricultural deities and Frazer's spirit-vs-god distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Agricultural/ corn-related beings split into 'spirits' (restricted to a definite department, generic names, lacking individual histories) and 'gods' (proper names, broader powers, fixed myths/representations). Agricultural gods often connect with the Underworld because seed germinates underground.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct citation: Sir James Frazer's distinction: spirits 'are restricted in their operations to definite departments of nature... names are general, not proper...' versus gods who 'bear individual or proper names... their individual characters and histories are fixed by current myths...' Apply this criterion when classifying whether a figure is a local spirit, an identified cult god, or has been elevated from spirit to god.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corn-spirit: wandering, abodes, and mythic resurrection motifs
rubrics_metrics.description: The corn-spirit is conceived as resident in or watching the growing grain; when the crop is cut it must 'materialize' elsewhere and wander until the next growth, giving rise to myths of searching and return (e.g., Demeter seeking Persephone, Isis seeking Osiris). Persephone/Osiris may represent the sown seed lying dormant in the Underworld and later resurrected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the corn-spirit model to interpret myths of abduction/search/resurrection and seasonal cycles; rituals (sheaf rites) and folklore (sheaf as corn-spirit) are evidence of this animistic origin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fire-gods: domestic/mechanical/smith aspects and relation to metalwork
rubrics_metrics.description: Fire deities often arise from animistic interpretations of fire and later become departmental gods tied to domestic hearths, mechanical arts, and metalworking (smithy). Some are linked with cosmic fire/lightning and may be partially absorbed by sun-gods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Agni (Vedic fire, guide of souls, regulator of sacrifices), Hephaestus/Vulcan (artificer, lame smith), Loki (fire-demon aspects), Xiuhtecutli (Mexican hearth/fire-god). Note the historical constraint that smith-type fire-gods arise after metallurgy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wind-gods: spectrum from gentle breeze to tempest personified
rubrics_metrics.description: Winds are widely personified: gentle breezes and favourable winds may be deified as benign figures (Pan, Favonius), while violent winds/storms become powerful, sometimes martial deities (Maruts, Boreas, Odin aspects). Wind-deities can be independently important or subordinate to a pantheon's supreme god.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for cultural variants: Hindu Maruts, Greek Boreas/Æolus, Mexican Tezcatlipoca as 'Lord of the Night Wind'. Note how wind's perceived qualities (shifting, deceptive, life-giving/destroying) map to mythic attributes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Earth-gods / Earth-Mother: universality and fertility rites
rubrics_metrics.description: The earth is commonly personified as a universal Earth-Mother who produces and restores life; myths often pair Sky-Father and Earth-Mother and yield widespread fertility rites, food-offerings, and symbolic acts of communion with soil.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Gæa, Mama Allpa, Ops, rites like 'Tasting of the Soil' for Centeotl. Use earth-mother criteria to identify maternal/producer imagery, rituals of communion with soil, and mythic motifs of death and renewal tied to the ground.

rubrics_metrics.name: Folk festival embodiment: the Burry Man as plant-spirit representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Local folk customs may preserve animistic/vegetation-spirit beliefs: the Burry Man (dressed in burrs and taken from door to door) represents a tree- or plant-spirit embodied in human form as part of harvest celebrations and community ritual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Burry Man example demonstrates continuity from ancient corn/plant-spirit beliefs to modern festival practice. Use such festival accounts as ethnographic evidence for the persistence of departmental spirit motifs and for interpreting communal rites of renewal and payment/tribute.
